nameStory: These tiny shrimp-like creatures earned the name 'scud' from their distinctive darting, scudding motion through the water - like clouds scudding quickly across the sky. The 'tide-pool' part tells you exactly where to look for them, as they're perfectly adapted to life in the rocky pools left behind when the ocean retreats.
description: Tide-pool scuds are tiny, shrimp-like crustaceans that look like miniature translucent commas swimming sideways through tide pools. These small amphipods (am-FIH-pods - meaning 'different feet') grow to about half an inch long and have flattened, curved bodies that help them navigate tight spaces between rocks and seaweed. Their bodies are typically clear to pale green, making them surprisingly hard to spot until they start moving with their characteristic jerky, darting motions.

idTips.label: Sideways Swimming
idTips.description: Watch for the telltale sideways swimming motion - they dart and dash through the water lying on their sides, never swimming upright like true shrimp

idTips.label: Curved Body Shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly comma-shaped or C-curved, flattened from side to side like it's been gently squeezed, giving it a hunchbacked appearance

idTips.label: Translucent Coloring
idTips.description: Body appears glassy and nearly transparent with a slight greenish or whitish tint - you can often see dark spots of their internal organs through the clear body wall

idTips.label: Size and Texture
idTips.description: About the size of a rice grain to small paperclip, feeling smooth and slippery when gently caught (though they're quite delicate)

idTips.label: Antenna Movement
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae constantly wave and probe ahead as they move, creating tiny currents you can sometimes see disturbing algae particles

idTips.label: Habitat Behavior
idTips.description: Often found clinging to or hiding under seaweed and rocks, quickly scattering when their cover is disturbed

habitat: Look for tide-pool scuds in rocky intertidal zones along New England's coast, especially in pools that retain seawater during low tide. They thrive in areas with plenty of seaweed like rockweed and sea lettuce, often hiding beneath these algae or in crevices between barnacle-covered rocks. You'll find them from the splash zone down to the low tide mark, particularly where there's good water circulation but protection from crashing waves.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures warm up, making this an excellent time to spot them darting around tide pools. Look for increased numbers as they begin their breeding season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with largest populations visible in tide pools. Young scuds appear as tiny translucent specks, much smaller than adults.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active but may be deeper in crevices as storms increase. Often found in larger aggregations sheltering together under seaweed.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to spot, typically hiding deep in rock crevices or under thick algae mats. Present but sluggish in their movements.

funFact: Tide-pool scuds are actually fantastic parents - the females carry their eggs in a special brood pouch on their belly, and after hatching, the tiny babies continue to ride around in mom's pouch like passengers on a sideways underwater bus until they're big enough to swim solo!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with tiny shrimp or baby fish, but remember the key difference: scuds always swim on their sides while shrimp swim upright. If it's darting around sideways like it's doing a perpetual backstroke, you've found a scud!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tide-pool' scuds, these creatures can actually tolerate a wide range of salinity levels, which is why you might occasionally spot them in brackish areas where streams meet the sea. This adaptability makes them important indicator species for coastal ecosystem health.
compareHints: Tide-pool scuds differ from their freshwater cousin, the common scud (Gammarus fasciatus), by their tolerance for salt water and slightly more robust build. Unlike Gammarus mucronatus, which prefers deeper waters, tide-pool scuds are specifically adapted for the harsh conditions of intertidal pools with their ability to handle rapid temperature and salinity changes. The tide-pool species also tends to be more translucent than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gammarus fasciatus is distinguished from its saltwater cousin the Tide-pool Scud by its smaller size and freshwater habitat, while Gammarus mucronatus tends to be slightly larger and more robust.
Pointed Scuds are distinguished from their cousin the Tide-pool Scud by their more prominent spines and pointed body segments that give them their name.
